To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

HPV‐negative LSLS are more likely to persist, progress to high‐grade disease, and require treatment than HPV‐positive LSLS, and that HPV‐negative women with LSLS are at increased risk for high‐grade disease compared with women who are HPV‐positive and have LSLS.

HPV‐negative LS IL is associated with a higher prevalence of cytologic high‐grade squamous epithelial lesions (HSIL) at 24 months than HPV‐positive LSIL, and the prevalence of HSIL at 24 months was not associated with the HPV‐negative LS I L cytologic pattern.

HPV‐negative, low-grade squamous intraepitheial lesions (LSILs) are not likely to progress, but may be associated with a slightly increased risk of high-grade squamous intra-epithelial lesions and invasive cervical cancer.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the study of the structure and properties of the human papilloma viruses (HPVs), which are responsible for the development of cervical cancer.
the development of new methods for the detection and identification of viruses, including the human immunodeficiency viruses (HIV) which cause acquired immune deficiency syndrome (AIDS).
the development and application of novel methods for the analysis of complex biological systems and the design of novel therapeutics and vaccines.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

HPV‐negative LSLI are a heterogeneous group of lesions with a variety of etiologies, including HPV, but also including other etiologies, such as reactive and inflammatory processes, and that HPV‐negative women with LSIL are at increased risk for high‐grade squamous epithelial lesions and cervical cancer.
women with HPV‐negative LSLI should be managed as women without LSIL.

the majority of women with HPV‐negative, LSIL have no evidence of underlying cervical neoplasia, and that a subset of HPV‐negative, atypical squamous cell of undetermined significance (ASCUS) have evidence of cervical neoplasms.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the majority of women with HPV‐negative LSI are not at high risk for progression to cervical intraepithelial neoplasia (CIN) grade II or greater.
HPV‐negative LSI L are associated with a low rate of progression to high‐grade lesions, but a higher rate of regression compared with HPV‐positive LSIL.
HPV‐negative LSIls are a heterogeneous group of lesions, with some being associated with high‐risk HPV and other being associated with low‐risk HPV.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the majority of women with HPV-negative LSIL have normal colposcopy and do not progress to high-grade squamous intraepitheilial lesions (HSIL) or cervical cancer.
HPV‐negative LSLS are a heterogeneous group, and the clinical significance of HPV‐negativity in LSLS is dependent on the histologic subtype of the lesion.
women with HPV‐negative LSILEs are not at increased risk for high‐grade squamous lesions or invasive cancer, and therefore, they can be managed conservatively.
